title: Installed isn't the same as loaded
prompt:
A *package* is a bundle of extra functions someone else has written. The
`dplyr` package adds `filter()`, `mutate()` and others that generated code
uses constantly.

Yesterday you ran:

```
install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)
```

Today, in a fresh R session, you run `mutate()` and get:

```
Error in mutate(patients, map = (sbp + 2 * dbp)/3) :
  could not find function "mutate"
```

What's missing?
hint:
Of yesterday's two lines, which one has a lasting effect, and which lasts
only until R closes?

options.text: `library(dplyr)` — it has to be run again in every new session
options.feedback:
Right. `install.packages()` downloads the package onto your computer,
once. `library()` opens it for this session, and closing R puts it
away again. It's the difference between installing an app and opening
it.

That's why generated code usually starts with a few `library()` lines,
and why this is the error you get when they're missing.

It's still installed — that lasts. What resets with every new session
is whether it's *loaded*, and loading is `library(dplyr)`.

It's spelled correctly. "Could not find function" here means R hasn't
been told where to look: the package that contains `mutate()` isn't
loaded yet.

title: Which error needs installing?
prompt: Which of these errors is fixed by running `install.packages()`?
hint:
One of them says R couldn't find the package at all. The other says it
couldn't find a function.

options.feedback:
Right. R looked for `dplyr` on this computer and found nothing — so
either it was never installed, or the name is misspelled. It's worth
checking the spelling before installing anything: `dplyrr` gives this
same message.

That one usually means the package is installed but not loaded, so the
fix is `library(dplyr)`, not installing it again.

`library()` can only open a package that's already on your computer.
"There is no package called…" means it isn't there to open.

title: Quotes, or no quotes?
prompt:
Which of these four lines fails?

```
install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages(dplyr)
library(dplyr)
library("dplyr")
```
hint: Without quotes, R treats a word as the name of a variable.

options.feedback:
Right: *object 'dplyr' not found*. Without quotes, R looks for a
variable called `dplyr`, and there isn't one. `install.packages()`
needs the name as text, in quotes.

`library()` is the odd one out: it accepts the name with or without
quotes. You'll see both in generated code, which is part of why this
catches people.

This is the correct way to write it — the package name as text, in
quotes.

This works. `library()` is unusual in accepting a package name without
quotes.
This works too — `library()` accepts the name with or without quotes.

title: The message that looks like a problem
prompt:
Running `library(dplyr)` prints this:

```
Attaching package: 'dplyr'

The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
```

Did something go wrong?
hint:
It doesn't say "Error" anywhere. What might "masked" mean if two packages
both have a function called `filter`?

options.text: No — dplyr has its own versions of those functions, and they now take priority
options.feedback:
Right. It's a message, not an error. Base R already has a function
called `filter()`, and so does dplyr. When two loaded packages share a
name, the one loaded last wins — so from now on, `filter()` means
dplyr's. The old one is "masked": still there, but hidden behind it.

It's worth reading rather than scrolling past, as the next exercise
shows.

It loaded fine. Nothing here says "Error". It's a message telling you
which existing functions dplyr's own versions now replace.

options.text: Yes — some of your data has been hidden
options.feedback:
"Masked" refers to functions, not data. Your data frames are
untouched. Where two packages have a function with the same name,
dplyr's version now takes priority.

title: An error that points the wrong way
prompt:
In a fresh session, someone forgot `library(dplyr)` and ran:

```
filter(patients, sbp > 140)
```

```
Error: object 'sbp' not found
```

`sbp` is spelled correctly, and it's a column in `patients`. What actually
went wrong?
hint:
Think back to the last exercise. Without dplyr loaded, whose `filter()`
runs?

options.text: Without `library(dplyr)`, R ran base R's own `filter()`, which doesn't look inside data frames
options.feedback:
Right — and it's one of the most misleading errors you'll meet. Base R
has its own `filter()`, the one from the "masked" message, built for
something else entirely. It doesn't know `sbp` is a column, so it goes
looking for a variable called `sbp` and doesn't find one.

The error points at `sbp`, but the real problem is a missing
`library()` line. When an error doesn't make sense, check that the
packages are loaded before you check your spelling.

It's spelled correctly — which is exactly what makes this confusing.
The error points at `sbp`, but the cause is that dplyr isn't loaded,
so a different `filter()` ran.

If `patients` were missing, the error would name `patients`. It names
`sbp` because the wrong `filter()` ran — base R's, which dplyr would
normally mask.

If it weren't installed, `library(dplyr)` would say "there is no
package called 'dplyr'". Here the package was simply never loaded.

title: Two colons
prompt:
Generated code often writes things like this:

```r
dplyr::filter(patients, discharged)
```

What does `dplyr::` mean?
hint: Read it left to right: a package's name, then a function's name.
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

options.text: Use the `filter()` from the dplyr package, specifically
options.feedback:
Right. `package::function` names exactly which function you mean. It
removes any doubt about which `filter()` runs, and it works even
without `library(dplyr)`, as long as dplyr is installed.

That's why careful generated code uses it: the problem from the last
exercise can't happen.

There's no function called `dplyr()`. The part before `::` is a
package's name, saying where to find the function that comes after.

`::` never installs anything. It only says which package's `filter()`
you mean — and the package has to be installed already.

title: Column names without $
prompt:
Since module 7 you've written `patients$sbp`, because `sbp` on its own
doesn't exist. But generated code writes this, and it works:

```r
filter(patients, sbp > 140)
```

Why?
hint: Look at what `filter()` is given first.
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

options.text: `filter()` is given `patients` first, so it looks for `sbp` among that data frame's columns
options.feedback:
Right. dplyr's functions take the data frame first, and inside them
you can write column names on their own. `filter()` knows to look for
`sbp` in `patients`.

The module 7 rule still holds everywhere else. Outside these
functions, `sbp` on its own is still "object not found" — which is
exactly what went wrong two exercises ago, when base R's `filter()`
ran instead of dplyr's.

It still holds everywhere outside functions like this one. `sbp` on
its own, in ordinary code, is still "object not found". dplyr's
functions are an exception because they're handed the data frame
first.

No new variable is created. `filter()` looks up `sbp` among the
columns of the data frame it was given.

title: The same filter, a different answer
prompt:
Patient 3's systolic is missing. In module 8, the square-bracket version
of this filter gave three rows, one of them an invented patient.

```r
filter(patients, sbp > 140)
```

How many rows does dplyr's `filter()` give?
hint:
`sbp > 140` is still `TRUE FALSE NA FALSE TRUE`. The question is what
`filter()` does with the `NA`.
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

options.feedback:
Right. `filter()` keeps only the rows where the answer is TRUE, and
drops the rest — including any where it's `NA`. No phantom patient.

That's safer, but notice it's also silent: the 71-year-old disappears
without a word, the way `t.test()` dropped a missing value in module
10. Same data, same question, two tools, two different answers —
square brackets give three rows, `filter()` gives two. Knowing which
tool the code used tells you which to expect.

options.text: 3 — the two high readings, plus a row that's entirely `NA`
options.feedback:
That's what square brackets gave in module 8. dplyr's `filter()`
handles the `NA` differently: it drops that row rather than inventing
one.

options.text: 3 — including the 71-year-old, with a blank blood pressure
options.feedback:
`filter()` keeps only the rows where the answer is TRUE. For the
71-year-old the answer is `NA`, so that row is dropped.

title: Filtering with filter()
prompt: Using `filter()`, keep only the patients who have been discharged.
hint:
The `discharged` column is already TRUE for exactly the rows you want.
Inside `filter()`, you can write the column's name on its own.
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

solution.why:
The same result as `patients[patients$discharged, ]` from module 8 —
shorter, and without needing `patients$` inside. Both are correct; the
difference is mostly how they read.

checks.on_fail: Not the three discharged patients yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
In quotes, `"discharged"` is just a piece of text, not the column.
Inside `filter()`, write the column's name without quotes:
`discharged`.

title: And then
prompt:
`|>` is the *pipe*. It takes what's on its left and hands it to the
function on its right, as that function's first argument. Read it as
*and then*:

```r
patients |> filter(discharged)
```

*Take `patients`, and then keep the discharged ones.* It's the same as
`filter(patients, discharged)`. You'll also see `%>%`, an older pipe that
does the same job.

Write the last exercise as a pipe.
hint:
The pipe hands `patients` to `filter()` for you. Inside the brackets, you
only need the condition.
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

solution.why:
With one step, the pipe doesn't save much. Its value shows when steps
stack up — *take this, and then filter it, and then add a column, and
then keep two columns* — each on its own line, read top to bottom.
That's how most generated tidyverse code is written.

checks.on_fail: Not the three discharged patients yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
The pipe already hands `patients` to `filter()` as its first argument,
so writing it again inside the brackets gives it twice. Inside, write
only the condition: `filter(discharged)`.

title: A column that wasn't kept
prompt:
`mutate()` is dplyr's way to add a column. You run:

```r
mutate(patients, map = (sbp + 2 * dbp) / 3)
```

Afterwards, does `patients` have a `map` column?
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

options.text: No — `mutate()` hands back a new data frame, and nothing stored it
options.feedback:
Right. dplyr's functions never change the data frame you give them;
they hand back a new one. To keep it, you store it:
`patients <- mutate(patients, map = (sbp + 2 * dbp) / 3)`.

That's why generated tidyverse code so often starts with
`patients <- patients |> …`. It's the same idea as module 8: filtering
never changed the original either.

That's how `patients$map <- …` behaved in module 9. `mutate()` works
differently: it hands back a new data frame, and unless you store it,
it's printed and gone.

options.text: Yes, but only until the session ends
options.feedback:
It isn't there at all afterwards. `mutate()` handed back a new data
frame, and nothing stored it.

title: Reading a pipeline
prompt:
This is the shape most generated tidyverse code takes. `select()` keeps
only the columns you name.

```r
patients |>
  filter(!is.na(sbp)) |>
  mutate(map = (sbp + 2 * dbp) / 3) |>
  select(age, map)
```

What comes out?
hint: Read it top to bottom, saying *and then* at each pipe.
setup:
library(dplyr)
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

options.feedback:
Right. Take `patients`, *and then* keep the rows where `sbp` isn't
missing — four — *and then* add MAP, *and then* keep only `age` and
`map`. Each line is one step, read in the order it's written.

And because nothing is stored, `patients` itself is exactly as it was.

The first step drops the patient whose systolic is missing, so four
rows are left by the time `select()` runs.
The last step, `select(age, map)`, keeps only those two columns.

`select()` keeps every column you name, and it names two: `age` and
`map`.
